concept.technique_name: percent of a total then ratio approximation

examples.problem_statement: Questions are based on the accompanying data for College X. [From the graphs: College X has 200 adjunct faculty and 250 non-adjunct faculty; 2 percent of the adjunct faculty and 12 percent of the non-adjunct faculty are in the engineering field.] There are 275 students in the field of engineering at College X. Approximately what is the ratio of the number of students in engineering to the number of faculty in engineering? Select a single answer choice: (A) 8 to 1 (B) 10 to 1 (C) 12 to 1 (D) 14 to 1 (E) 20 to 1

solution.description: Read off the graph the two percentages that apply to engineering: 2 percent of the adjunct faculty and 12 percent of the non-adjunct faculty.
Apply the adjunct percentage to the 200 adjunct faculty to get the number of adjunct faculty in engineering.
Apply the non-adjunct percentage to the 250 non-adjunct faculty to get the number of non-adjunct faculty in engineering.
Add the two faculty counts to get the total number of faculty in engineering.
Form the ratio asked for, students in engineering to faculty in engineering.
Estimate by rounding both terms to numbers that divide evenly, then reduce the ratio to lowest terms.

key_reminders: A percent shown on a graph must be applied to that group's own total, not to a combined total.
Counts for two separate groups are added before the ratio is formed.
When the question says 'approximately', round both ratio terms to a pair that divides evenly.
common_mistakes: Adding the percentages (2\% + 12\%) and applying the sum to one total instead of computing 2\% of 200 and 12\% of 250 separately.
Applying 2 percent to the 250 non-adjunct group and 12 percent to the 200 adjunct group, swapping the two faculty categories.
Dividing 275 by only one of the faculty counts (4 or 30) instead of by the total 34.

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices. Frederick the Great of Prussia was known for his (i) _________ under fire during his military victories; however, when confronting issues of domestic policy, this equilibrium sometimes failed him. He was often (ii) _________ with his ministers, who never knew when they might be subjected to one of his tirades. Blank (i): intrepidity / cruelty / sangfroid. Blank (ii): fascist / mercurial / vainglorious.

solution.description: Locate the clue: the sentence calls the quality in blank (i) 'this equilibrium', so the word the second clause reuses is the anchor for both blanks.
Because 'this equilibrium' refers back to blank (i), the first blank must have the same meaning as equilibrium, not the opposite one the sentence's structure tempts you toward.
Apply the pivot: 'however' plus 'this equilibrium sometimes failed him' flips the direction, so the second blank must be opposite in meaning to equilibrium.
Choose from each column the word that matches the direction just fixed: composure for blank (i) and volatility for blank (ii).

key_reminders: A demonstrative phrase such as 'this equilibrium' points back at the earlier blank and defines it.
'However' reverses direction for the clause that follows it, not for the clause it refers back to.
In a two-blank text completion the two blanks can point in opposite directions from the same clue word.
common_mistakes: Treating 'however' as reversing blank (i) as well, and so making the first blank the opposite of equilibrium.
Picking a blank (i) word that fits 'under fire' by association (intrepidity, bravery) rather than one that matches the clue word equilibrium.

concept.technique_name: mean of combined equal-sized lists versus median
concept.sub_category: average and median of a combined frequency distribution

examples.problem_statement: Compare Quantity A and Quantity B. Frequency Distribution for List X: number 1, 2, 3, 5 with frequency 10, 20, 18, 12. Frequency Distribution for List Y: number 6, 7, 8, 9 with frequency 24, 17, 10, 9. List X and list Y each contain 60 numbers. The average (arithmetic mean) of the numbers in list X is 2.7, and the average of the numbers in list Y is 7.1. List Z contains 120 numbers: the 60 numbers in list X and the 60 numbers in list Y. Quantity A: the average of the 120 numbers in list Z. Quantity B: the median of the 120 numbers in list Z. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.description: Note that lists X and Y contribute the same count of numbers to list Z, which is what lets the two given averages be combined directly.
Because the two lists are the same size, average the two individual averages to get the average of the 120 numbers in list Z.

solution.operation: 120 \text{ numbers} \Rightarrow \text{median} = \text{average of the two middle numbers}
solution.description: Since list Z holds an even count of numbers, its median is the average of the two middle values once the numbers are placed in increasing order.

Check the two distributions: every one of the 60 numbers in list X is at most 5 and every one of the 60 numbers in list Y is at least 6, so the 60th and 61st values in order are the largest of X and the smallest of Y.
Average those two middle numbers to obtain the median of list Z.
Compare the median against the average and pick the larger quantity.

examples.answer: Choice B: Quantity B is greater.

key_reminders: The average of two combined lists equals the average of their averages only when the lists contain the same count of numbers.
For an even count of values the median is the average of the two middle values in increasing order.
When every value of one list is below every value of another, the split point of the ordered combined list falls between them.
common_mistakes: Averaging 2.7 and 7.1 with unequal weights, or summing them without dividing by 2.
Taking the median of list Z to be a single middle value rather than the average of the 60th and 61st numbers.
Reading the median off the frequency table of one list alone (for example calling it 5 or 6) instead of averaging the two middle numbers 5 and 6.
